Studio 9 — Transformation — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2D Studio Art 2 · CPALMS 0101310 · Grades 9–12 · full-year, async Canvas Cycle: Q3 · Studio 9 of 18 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week Content focus (Course Map): Stylization, simplification, abstraction from observation Featured artist: Georgia O'Keeffe — Autumn Trees, The Maple, 1924 (public domain, embedded); Rose, 1957 (in-copyright, linked out) Studio Project / ladder rung: From Study to Stylization — variation / transformation rung Teacher model: async students with a live teacher who grades, holds office hours, answers email. Every page is completable independently.

Six lessons in this Studio

  1. Where Observation Becomes Invention (Observe) — EQ, the abstraction journey, the core idea.
  2. Georgia O'Keeffe: A Career of Looking Closer (Investigate) — her path from representational work to magnification; DAIJ criticism modeled.
  3. The Abstraction Ladder (Skill Builder A) — realistic, simplified, stylized, non-representational → Skill Builder 1.
  4. Cropping & Magnification (Skill Builder B) — framing and scale as abstraction tools → Skill Builder 2.
  5. Plan & Create — choose subject, plan the transformation, VR session, AI awareness, begin the artwork.
  6. Refine, Reflect & Present — self-critique (DAIJ), artist statement, rubric, submission checklist.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q3 map set — verify exact wording at cpalms.org before quoting)

  • VA.912.C.1.x — Use critical-thinking and art-criticism vocabulary to describe, analyze, and interpret works (DAIJ applied to O'Keeffe in Lesson 2, and to the student's own progression in Lesson 6).
  • VA.912.C.3.x — Analyze how the elements of art and principles of design communicate ideas, here specifically how simplification, exaggeration, and stylization carry a subject's essence.
  • VA.912.S.2.x — Develop skills and techniques through deliberate studio practice (the abstraction ladder and the cropping/magnification skill builders).
  • VA.912.S.3.x — Apply various methods of critique to works in progress and completed works to inform revision (the Lesson 6 self-critique and progression review).
  • VA.912.O.3.x — Use organizational structures and functions to create unified compositions that carry intended meaning across a deliberate transformation.
  • VA.912.H.3.x — Examine how an individual artist's body of work reflects a developing personal style over time (O'Keeffe's career arc from representational still life to magnified abstraction).
  • VA.912.F.3.x — Consider innovation and technology in the creative process (VR abstraction-stage practice; factual AI-awareness on abstraction and observation).

Remaining Q3 map strands are carried across Studios 10–12 (Visual Storytelling, Design for Communication, Beyond Reality). See the course-shared standards tracker.

Texas TEKS Extension (19 TAC §117.302, Art Level I — optional/extension cross-reference)

  • 117.302(c)(1)(A) — consider concepts/ideas from direct observation, original sources, and imagination for original artwork (the whole Studio: an anchor observational drawing carried through to an invented stylized or abstract piece).
  • 117.302(c)(3)(A) — compare/contrast historical and contemporary styles, themes, and trends (O'Keeffe's career arc from representational still life to magnified abstraction, Lesson 2).
  • 117.302(c)(4)(B) — evaluate/analyze artwork via a verbal or written critique method: describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate (Lesson 2 modeled critique of O'Keeffe's work; Lesson 6 self-critique of the student's own progression).

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Look & Learn ≈ 250 min): Lesson 1 (~45) · Lesson 2 (~50) · Lesson 3 + Skill Builder 1 (~50 + 30) · Lesson 4 + Skill Builder 2 (~50 + 30). Reading + guided practice + two completion sketches. Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Lesson 5 (~60) · Quiz (~15) · VR Session (~25) · Lesson 6 (~55) · Studio Project studio time and refinement (~95, self-paced across the week).

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Studio Project (anchor drawing, transitional stages, final piece) + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Skill Builder 1, Skill Builder 2, and the VR session are completion-scored; the quiz is auto-graded. This keeps the cycle inside the 500:1 arithmetic.

Quiz answer key ("Abstraction & O'Keeffe")

1-B · 2-C · 3-C · 4-C · 5-B · 6-False · 7 (Essence→the core visual idea that keeps a simplified form recognizable; Exaggeration→pushing one quality of a subject further than reality shows it; Cropping→choosing what falls inside the frame and what is cut away; Magnification→enlarging a form's scale so the viewer sees it differently than at life size) · 8-B.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • Georgia O'Keeffe (d. 1986) — Autumn Trees, The Maple, 1924. Public domain in the US (published 1924). PD status confirmed 2026-09-18 (US publication 1924). Embedded inline in Lesson 1 with attribution + source note. File copied from the provided archive (Studio Art 2 Images / Unit 8) into Studio-09/images/okeeffe-autumn-trees-maple-1924.jpg.
  • Georgia O'Keeffe (d. 1986) — Rose, 1957. In-copyright. NOT embedded. Lesson 2 describes the work and links out to the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum's Access O'Keeffe catalogue record for Rose, ca. 1957: https://access-ok.okeeffemuseum.org/object/1046/ (verified 2026-09-18). Build agents have no network access to verify.
  • Technique reference images (2026-07-15 revision) — Lesson 3 and Lesson 4 now embed real, license-verified reference images in place of the earlier flat SVG diagrams, per the reviewer's "no clip art, real images" note. All four are hotlinked from Wikimedia Commons with on-page attribution; direct file URLs and license pages confirmed to resolve at build time:
  • Realistic (Lesson 3, Stage 1): Becca, Maple Leaf Macro — CC BY 2.0.
  • Simplified (Lesson 3, Stage 2): Siebold & Zuccarini, Flora Japonica Tab. 145, 1870 — public domain (the plain line-outline leaf drawing on the plate, labeled 9, is the reference point named in the caption).
  • Stylized (Lesson 3, Stage 3): Sumikiri-kaku ni hitoha momiji, a traditional Japanese maple-leaf family crest (kamon) — public domain.
  • Non-representational (Lesson 3, Stage 4): Arthur Dove, Nature Symbolized, 1911 — public domain (d. 1946; published before 1931).
  • Lesson 4's full-object/cropped-magnified comparison uses one real photograph, Leon Brooks' Daisy flower (public domain), shown twice: once whole, once cropped and enlarged via CSS object-position/transform:scale on the same unaltered file, so the "nothing was distorted, only framed" point is demonstrated with a genuine photograph rather than two different illustrations. Verify all five Commons URLs still resolve at deploy.

Every page is completable independently.

Six lessons in this Studio

  1. A Story With No Words (Observe) — EQ, the Muybridge sequential-photograph demonstration, sequence vs. single image.
  2. Two Ways to Tell It (Investigate) — Jacob Lawrence + Norman Rockwell; critique method modeled.
  3. Storyboarding & Sequencing (Skill Builder) — three-beat structure, pacing → Skill Builder 1.

  • VA.912.C.1.x — Use critical-thinking and art-criticism vocabulary to describe, analyze, and interpret works (critique method, applied to Lawrence and Rockwell).

  • VA.912.S.2.x — Develop skills and techniques through deliberate studio practice (storyboarding, single-image composition).

Six lessons in this Studio

  1. A Painting of Nothing (Observe) — EQ, abstract vs. non-objective, Kandinsky's core idea.
  2. What Works? (Investigate) — Frankenthaler + Arcay; critique method modeled on non-objective work.

  4. Composing with Pure Elements (Skill Builder) — rhythm, balance, color emotion → Skill Builder 2.

Studio 14 — Art & Society — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2D Studio Art 2 · CPALMS 0101310 · Grades 9–12 · full-year, async Canvas Cycle: Q4 · Studio 14 of 18 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week Content focus (Course Map): Social commentary, visual communication, image + text + audience Featured artists: Barbara Kruger (living, in-copyright, linked out); Shepard Fairey (living, in-copyright, linked out). No PD embed available for this Studio (source folder "Until 14" is a typo for Unit 14 and contains no usable PD images). Studio Project / ladder rung: A Cause Worth Making — invention rung, an original argument-driven artwork Teacher model: async students with a live teacher who grades, holds office hours, answers email. Every page is completable independently.

Six lessons in this Studio

  1. Can an Image Change a Mind? (Observe) — EQ, persuasion vs. propaganda, the core idea. Leads with an original CSS agitprop-style concept visual (no PD image available).
  2. Kruger & Fairey (Investigate) — critique process modeled on both artists; both link out.
  3. Message & Audience (Skill Builder A) — image-text vs. caption, naming an audience, slogan economy → Skill Builder 1.
  4. Responsible Commentary (Skill Builder B) — fact vs. opinion, arguing the idea not the person, AI-awareness on manipulated images → Skill Builder 2.
  5. Plan & Create — choose cause, plan (including a peer-pairing planning step, Part 2 Step 2b), VR session, AI awareness, begin the artwork.
  6. Refine, Reflect & Present — self-critique (critique process + fairness check), artist statement (with AI disclosure), rubric, submission checklist.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q4 map set — verify exact wording at cpalms.org before quoting)

  • VA.912.C.3.x — Analyze how art communicates ideas about social, cultural, or political issues; assess the artist's intent and responsibility to an audience.
  • VA.912.S.3.x — Apply advanced skills and techniques (image-text composition, appropriation) to produce a work of personal or social significance.
  • VA.912.O.1.x — Use structural elements and organizational principles (contrast, emphasis, hierarchy) to focus a viewer's attention and message.
  • VA.912.H.3.x — Examine how artists use their work to reflect on and respond to contemporary social conditions.
  • VA.912.F.3.x — Evaluate the impact of technology (image manipulation, AI tools) on the creation and credibility of visual messages.

Remaining Q4 map strands are carried across Studios 13, 15–18. See the course-shared standards tracker.

Texas TEKS Extension (19 TAC §117.302, Art Level I — optional/extension cross-reference)

  • 117.302(c)(2)(A) — use visual solutions to create original artwork through direct observation, original sources, experience, narration, and imagination (the Studio Project: an original argument-driven artwork built from the student's own cause and imagery).
  • 117.302(c)(3)(A) — compare/contrast historical and contemporary styles, themes, trends (Lesson 2's Kruger/Fairey pairing across decades; Lesson 3's historical propaganda poster alongside a contemporary slogan-economy example).
  • 117.302(c)(4)(B) — evaluate/analyze artwork via a critique method: describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate (Lesson 2 modeled critique; Lesson 6 self-critique and fairness check).

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Look & Learn ≈ 245 min): Lesson 1 (~45) · Lesson 2 (~50) · Lesson 3 + Skill Builder 1 (~50 + 30) · Lesson 4 + Skill Builder 2 (~50 + 20). Reading + guided practice + two completion sketches. Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Lesson 5 (~60) · Quiz (~15) · VR Session (~25) · Lesson 6 (~55) · Studio Project studio time and refinement (~95, self-paced across the week).

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Studio Project artwork + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Skill Builder 1, Skill Builder 2, and the VR session are completion-scored; the quiz is auto-graded. This keeps the cycle inside the 500:1 arithmetic.

Quiz answer key ("Persuasion, Kruger & Fairey")

1-B · 2-B · 3-C · 4-B · 5-C · 6-False · 7 (Appropriation→borrowing an existing image/style to make a new point; Audience→the specific group a work is built to reach; Direct address→speaking directly to the viewer, often using "you" or "your"; Fact→a claim that can be checked and verified) · 8-B.

Critique terminology note (2026-07-15 revision)

Studio 14 is not one of the four Studios (1, 5, 9, 13) that keeps the "DAIJ" acronym by name; Studio 13 is this quarter's sanctioned opener. Lesson 2 and the quiz use "critique" / "the critique process" instead, while keeping the same four-step describe/analyze/interpret/judge structure. Own-work critique (Lesson 6) never uses the acronym, only "critique," per owner decision, with no exceptions. See _REVISION-BRIEF.md §3.

Step 2b note (2026-07-15 revision, Studio-14-specific per _REVISION-BRIEF.md §8)

Lesson 5, Part 2 now includes a Step 2b: pair with one classmate who chose a related cause, compare one-sentence issue statements, and decide whether the two pieces will hang as a connected pair or combine into one shared piece. This is a brief planning conversation only, mirrored in canvas-items.md's Studio Project steps. It is the one deliberate, owner-approved exception to this course's solo-work rule; it does not make the Studio Project a joint submission or a shared grade. Each student still plans, makes, signs, and submits their own artwork and artist statement individually.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • Barbara Kruger (b. 1945, living) — in-copyright, LINK OUT only. Not embedded anywhere on the public Pages site. Lesson 1 leads with an original CSS agitprop-style concept graphic (band/type composition, no reproduction of any Kruger artwork). Lesson 2 describes Untitled (I shop therefore I am), 1987, in words and links to verified museum pages:
  • The Broad object page: https://www.thebroad.org/art/barbara-kruger/untitled-i-shop-therefore-i-am (replaced an unverifiable MoMA object URL; verified 2026-09-18)
  • The Broad artist page: https://www.thebroad.org/art/barbara-kruger (verified 2026-09-18)
  • Shepard Fairey (b. 1970, living) — in-copyright, LINK OUT only. Not embedded. Lesson 2 describes Rise Above and Glass Houses, 2010, in words and links to:
  • Official artist/OBEY site: https://obeygiant.com/ (verified 2026-09-18)
  • Smithsonian American Art Museum artist page: https://americanart.si.edu/artist/shepard-fairey-31857 (verified 2026-09-18)
  • The provided source folder is labeled "Until 14," a typo for Unit 14. Its contents were not used for embeds; no PD image exists for this Studio's featured artists (both are living). The agitprop panel (Lesson 1), the Kruger-formula demo (Lesson 2), the slogan-economy demo (Lesson 3), and the fact/opinion cards (Lesson 4) remain original HTML/CSS built with course design tokens. No AI-generated images anywhere in this Studio.
  • Technique reference images (2026-07-15 revision) — Lesson 3's "Image alone / Caption / Image-text" comparison now embeds two real, public-domain reference works in place of the earlier flat SVG icons, per the reviewer's "no clip art, real images" note:
  • Dorothea Lange, Migrant Mother, Nipomo, California, 1936 (Farm Security Administration; public domain, US government work), used for both the "Image alone" and "Caption" panels (the same photograph; the "Caption" panel adds its real original Library of Congress caption text to show the difference).
  • James Montgomery Flagg, I Want You for U.S. Army, 1917 (public domain; artist d. 1960, published before 1931), used for the "Image-text" panel, since the poster fuses text and image into a single argument. Both are hotlinked from Wikimedia Commons with on-page attribution, following the same hotlink convention as the course's other technique-diagram replacements. The Flagg poster is a historical recruitment artifact used strictly to illustrate the form of image-text fusion; it is not an endorsement of its message. Verify both Commons URLs still resolve at deploy.

AI-awareness compliance note

Lesson 4 (Skill Builder B) carries the required AI-awareness tie-in on manipulated images, factual and non-alarmist per house style: what AI image tools can and cannot verify, and the plain-disclosure expectation. Lesson 5 repeats a shorter, project-specific version tied to the Studio Project. The Studio Project rubric and artist-statement prompt (Lesson 6, canvas-items.md) require AI disclosure if used at any stage; the rubric's Artist Statement row treats a missing required disclosure as Beginning-level. No specific AI tool is named or required; this is awareness, not mandated tool use.

Design compliance

  • Brand chrome byte-consistent with the course shell (navy/cyan/gold, owl header). Accents limited to teal #1B8A7A and coral #D9583B; green retired; red reserved for the AI-awareness callouts (Lessons 4 and 5). No off-palette or other-subject colors. Hex audit run against _BUILD-CONVENTIONS.md sanctioned set (navy #0E1C42/#1a2340/#223a63; cyan #55C8E8/#a9e4f5; gold #C7922C/#9a6f16/#E7D3A1/#FBF1DC/#FDF3E3; teal #1B8A7A/#167567 + tints #E6F4F1/#D8EEE9/#CFE5DF/#EEF8F5/#F6FBFA/#7CC3B8/#7FD4C6; coral #D9583B/#A93B22 + tints #FBEEE9/#FBE6E0/#F0B39E; red (AI only) #C0392B/#E74C3C/#FDECEC/#8A1F16; neutral grays/white) across all six lessons; no banned rogue blue (#2196D0, #1B6A94, #C5DCE5, #E8F6FB) present.
  • No em dashes in student-facing text (title tags use — per convention, exempted). No giveaway answers (practice items never bold the target answer; correct-answer button position varied row to row). Commit-then-reveal accordions put the "do it in your notebook" instruction in the visible summary, not beside the answer. Every widget has a Reset. Correct-answer index varied across rows and across lessons.

Deployment notes

  • lesson-1.html … lesson-6.html → GitHub Pages; embed each in Canvas via iframe (see canvas-interactive-widgets). Deploy-ready; no preview banner. This Studio still has no local images/ folder: Kruger and Fairey remain link-out only (in-copyright), and Lesson 3's two new reference images (Migrant Mother; the Flagg poster) are hotlinked directly from Wikimedia Commons, consistent with the technique-diagram convention used elsewhere in the course.
  • canvas-items.md → build each item Canvas-native (Quiz as a Canvas Quiz; Skill Builders, VR, and Studio Project as Canvas Assignments).
  • Module intro/outro wrappers (Canvas-native quizzes) bracket the cycle per optima-canvas-assignments; built at module level, not in this Studio folder.
  • Before publishing: verify all four link-out URLs above resolve to the stated works/artists, and verify the two Lesson 3 Wikimedia Commons image URLs still resolve; if a URL has moved, replace with the current museum/artist collection page or Commons file for the same work.

Studio 15 — Experimental Studio — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2D Studio Art 2 · CPALMS 0101310 · Grades 9–12 · full-year, async Canvas Cycle: Q4 · Studio 15 of 18 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week Content focus (Course Map): Exploration, innovation, media combination Featured artists: None assigned this Studio. Lesson 2 offers two optional springboards revisiting artists already studied — Hannah Höch (Studio 6, in-copyright, linked out) and Georgia O'Keeffe (Studio 9, US-PD embed already used in that Studio; not re-embedded here) — framed through the lens of risk rather than technique. Students may reference any prior-Studio artist as a springboard; none is required. Studio Project / ladder rung: Risk Log: A Series of Experimental Works — invention rung (self-directed combination of prior techniques, no assigned model) Teacher model: async students with a live teacher who grades, holds office hours, answers email. Every page is completable independently.

Six lessons in this Studio

  1. Why Artists Experiment (Observe) — EQ, the materials-matrix/experiment-log visual, variable/control introduced conceptually.
  2. Studying Innovation (Investigate) — optional springboards (Höch, O'Keeffe) revisited through the lens of risk; the critique method applied to risk-taking. Lesson 2 now also offers a choice prompt: students critique either springboard artist, mirroring the Studio 1 "Watch It Work" pattern.
  3. Structured Experimentation (Skill Builder) — variable, control, honest documentation → Skill Builder 1.
  4. Combining Media Safely (Skill Builder) — layering order, safe vs. caution combinations, materials safety → Skill Builder 2.
  5. Plan & Create — design the series (the project brief's "strong series" traits now number four; see the 2026-07-15 revision note below), VR quick-experiment session, AI awareness, begin the Studio Project.
  6. Refine, Reflect & Present — self-critique on risk (the critique method), artist statement on risk/learning, rubric, submission checklist.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q4 map set — verify exact wording at cpalms.org before quoting)

  • VA.912.C.3.x — Evaluate and refine one's own work through structured critique and reflection on process (the critique method applied to risk, Lesson 6 self-critique).
  • VA.912.S.3.x — Demonstrate advanced skill and technique through deliberate, self-directed studio practice (structured experimentation, safe media combination).
  • VA.912.O.1.x (carried) — Apply the structural elements and organizational principles of art across novel, combined media contexts.
  • VA.912.H.3.x — Consider how innovation and departure from convention have shaped artists' contributions (Lesson 2 springboards).
  • VA.912.F.3.x — Consider the role of innovation, risk, and technology in the creative process, including factual AI-awareness (Lesson 5).

Remaining Q4 map strands are carried across Studios 13–18. See the course-shared standards tracker.

Texas TEKS Extension (19 TAC §117.302, Art Level I)

Optional/extension cross-reference, alongside the FL NGSSS set above (FL remains primary): - 117.302(c)(1)(A) — consider concepts/ideas from direct observation, original sources, experience, and imagination for original artwork (the Risk Log series is built entirely from the student's own trial-and-error experience). - 117.302(c)(2)(F) — demonstrate effective use of art media/tools (drawing, painting, printmaking, design, digital art) (Lessons 3–4's structured media combinations; the new dimensional/fiber-based technique requirement in Lesson 5). - 117.302(c)(4)(B) — evaluate/analyze artwork via a verbal or written critique method (describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate) (Lesson 2 critique of the springboard artists; Lesson 6 self-critique of risk). - 117.302(c)(4)(C) — build a physical/electronic portfolio evaluating personal artwork (the experiment log itself functions as process-documentation for the portfolio).

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Look & Learn ≈ 250 min): Lesson 1 (~45) · Lesson 2 (~50) · Lesson 3 + Skill Builder 1 (~50 + 30) · Lesson 4 + Skill Builder 2 (~50 + 25). Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Lesson 5 (~55) · Quiz (~10, shorter by design — process Studio, no artist recall) · VR Session (~20) · Lesson 6 (~55) · Studio Project studio time and refinement (~110, self-paced across the week, scaling three finished pieces from prior trials).

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Studio Project series (3+ pieces) + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 to 7 min/student, slightly higher than a single-piece Studio because the teacher reviews a short series and its log). Skill Builder 1, Skill Builder 2, and the VR session are completion-scored; the quiz is auto-graded. This keeps the cycle inside the 500:1 arithmetic.

Quiz answer key ("Experimentation & Iteration")

1-B · 2-B · 3-C · 4-True · 5-B · 6-B · 7 (Variable→the one factor deliberately changed between trials; Control→the factors deliberately held the same across trials; Iteration→repeating and adjusting a trial across a series, each informed by the last; Process documentation→a written and photographed record of what was tried and what happened).

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • No new artist images are embedded or introduced in Studio 15. This is a process/portfolio-style Studio per the Course Map and _STUDIO-SPECS.md Notes for build agents (Studios 8, 15, 16, 17, 18).
  • Lesson 1 lead visual: an original CSS/HTML "experiment log" table (five sample trials). No third-party image; not a reproduction of any real artist's notebook.
  • Lesson 2 references two artists already studied earlier in the course, framed as optional springboards:
  • Hannah Höch (d. 1978) — in-copyright, not embedded. Linked out to a verified museum page. Link is moma.org/artists/2675-hannah-hoch (the earlier id 2645 was wrong), verified 2026-09-18.
  • Georgia O'Keeffe — discussed in text only, not re-embedded (her US-PD 1924 work was already embedded and verified in Studio 9's teacher-cycle-plan; no new image file added here).
  • Lessons 3 and 4 lead visuals (variable/control diagram, layering-order swatches, safety cards) are original HTML/CSS built with course design tokens. No third-party images, no AI-generated images.
  • No images/ folder is needed for this Studio.

2026-07-15 revision note

  • DAIJ → critique. Studio 15 is not one of the four sanctioned quarter-opener Studios (1, 5, 9, 13), so every "DAIJ" reference is now plain "critique" / "the critique process" language: the Lesson 2 metadata strip ("Critique method"), the Lesson 2 walkthrough intro, and the Lesson 6 self-critique instruction. The four-step describe/analyze/interpret/judge structure is unchanged.
  • Lesson 2 "Watch It Work" choice. Added a "Now You Try" prompt letting students pick either springboard artist (Höch or O'Keeffe) to critique themselves, matching the Studio 1 pattern.
  • Quiz moved to Week 2. "Experimentation & Iteration" now falls in the Week 2 budget (was miscategorized as Week 1); the Lesson 2 "after this lesson" pointer and the Lesson 6 submission checklist were updated to match. The quiz stays short by design (7 questions, no artist recall).
  • Texas TEKS Extension added (see section above), 4 codes.
  • Intro wrapper now notes "(solo; no partner or group option)" in canvas-items.md.
  • Studio-15-specific content addition (brief §8): the Lesson 5 "strong series" traits list grew from three to four; the new 4th trait requires at least one piece in the series to use a dimensional or fiber-based technique (built-up modeling paste, torn fabric, or stitched thread). Mirrored into the "What makes a strong series" list in canvas-items.md. No new project was added; the Studio Project remains one series of 3+ pieces.
  • No clip-art replacement needed. Studio 15 has no .tech-demo icons and no featured-artist images. Its three lead visuals (the Lesson 1 experiment-log matrix, the Lesson 3 variable/control diagram and log template, and the Lesson 4 layering-order swatches and safety cards) are original CSS/HTML structural and data diagrams, not decorative clip art, consistent with _STUDIO-SPECS.md classifying Studio 15 as a process/portfolio Studio with CSS-original visuals. None were replaced with photographic images.

Design compliance

  • Brand chrome byte-consistent with the course shell (navy/cyan/gold, owl header). Accents limited to teal #1B8A7A and coral #D9583B; green retired; red reserved for the AI-awareness callout (Lesson 5) and the materials-safety callout (Lesson 4). No off-palette or other-subject colors.
  • Hex audit run against _BUILD-CONVENTIONS.md sanctioned set: navy #0E1C42/#1a2340/#223a63; cyan #55C8E8/#a9e4f5; gold #C7922C/#9a6f16/#E7D3A1/#FBF1DC/#FDF3E3; teal #1B8A7A/#167567/#E6F4F1/#D8EEE9/#CFE5DF/#EEF8F5/#F6FBFA/#7CC3B8/#7FD4C6; coral #D9583B/#A93B22/#FBEEE9/#FBE6E0/#F0B39E; red (AI/safety only) #C0392B/#E74C3C/#FDECEC/#8A1F16; plus neutral grays (#f4f6fa, #f8f9fc, #EEF1F8, #D0D9E8, #E1E7F0, #6b7a99, #666, #fff/#ffffff) and their gradient combinations. No banned blues (#2196D0, #1B6A94, #C5DCE5, #E8F6FB) and no green anywhere in the six lesson files.
  • No em dashes in student-facing text except the <title> tags (per convention). No giveaway answers (practice items never bold or pre-state the exact correct choice). Instruction-before-reveal accordions place the "do this in your notebook" instruction in the visible summary, not beside the answer. Every widget has a Reset. Studio 16 — Independent Investigation — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2D Studio Art 2 · CPALMS 0101310 · Grades 9–12 · full-year, async Canvas Cycle: Q4 · Studio 16 of 18 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week Content focus (Course Map): Research, planning, and artistic voice — the Capstone plan Featured artists: None assigned. Student chooses, using the approved source list (see HS Art Sources.docx: Smarthistory, Khan Academy Art History, the Met, Smithsonian Learning Lab, National Gallery of Art, Art Institute of Chicago, Rijksmuseum, MoMA, Tate, Crystal Bridges, Getty Education, Google Arts & Culture, Van Gogh Letters, JSTOR/Artstor). Studio Project / ladder rung: The Capstone Proposal — invention-prep rung (the written plan Studio 17 executes) Teacher model: async students with a live teacher who grades, holds office hours, answers email. Every page is completable independently.

Six lessons in this Studio

  1. What Do You Want to Say? (Observe) — EQ, no assigned artist, the four-stage planner (Interest → Research → Dialogue → Proposal).
  2. Researching an Artist Responsibly (Investigate) — primary vs. secondary sources, verifying facts, the AI-for-research-vs-making-the-art distinction.
  3. Finding & Vetting Sources (Skill Builder A) — the approved source list, the source-reliability checklist → Skill Builder 1: Research Notes.
  4. From Research to Proposal (Skill Builder B) — the four parts of a proposal, building a thesis sentence → Skill Builder 2: Thumbnail Sketches.
  5. Plan & Create — VR "curate an influences gallery," AI-awareness on making, begin drafting the proposal document.
  6. Refine, Reflect & Present — self-critique (the critique process applied to the proposal), artist statement guidance, rubric preview, submission checklist.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q4 map set — verify exact wording at cpalms.org before quoting)

  • VA.912.C.3.x — Analyze, interpret, and evaluate one's own work and process through structured critique and reflection (the critique process run on the student's own proposal, Lesson 6).
  • VA.912.S.3.x — Plan and develop skills and works through sustained inquiry and independent studio practice (the research-to-proposal arc).
  • VA.912.O.3.x — Apply organizational structure and a personal point of view when generating an original concept.
  • VA.912.H.3.x — Research and cite an artist's historical, cultural, or personal context accurately using verified sources.
  • VA.912.F.3.x — Use technology, including AI tools, thoughtfully and with awareness of its limits within the creative and research process.

Studio 16 is a process/portfolio studio (no artist folder, no artist-recall quiz item) per _STUDIO-SPECS.md Notes for build agents; it carries forward Q4's C.3/S.3/O.3/H.3/F.3 strand set from the course-shared standards tracker rather than introducing new content strands.

Texas TEKS Extension (19 TAC §117.302, Art Level I — optional/extension cross-reference)

  • 117.302(c)(1)(A) — consider concepts/ideas from direct observation, original sources, experience, and imagination for original artwork (the research-to-thesis arc: verified sources about a chosen artist feeding an original Capstone concept).
  • 117.302(c)(4)(B) — evaluate/analyze artwork via a verbal or written critique method: describe, analyze, interpret, evaluate (Lesson 6 self-critique run on the student's own proposal).
  • 117.302(c)(4)(C) — build a physical/electronic portfolio evaluating personal artwork (the Capstone Proposal document itself becomes a portfolio artifact ahead of Studio 17).

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Look & Learn ≈ 250 min): Lesson 1 (~45) · Lesson 2 (~50) · Lesson 3 + Skill Builder 1 (~50 + 30) · Lesson 4 + Skill Builder 2 (~55 + 25). Reading + guided practice + two completion tasks (research notes, thumbnails). Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Quiz (~15) · Lesson 5 (~55) · VR Session (~20) · drafting studio time (~90) · Lesson 6 (~50) · refinement and submission (~20, self-paced across the week).

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Capstone Proposal document + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Skill Builder 1 (Research Notes), Skill Builder 2 (Thumbnail Sketches), and the VR session are completion-scored; the quiz is auto-graded. This keeps the cycle inside the 500:1 arithmetic.

Note for teachers: this Studio's grading is necessarily more varied than a media-based Studio, since every student researches a different artist. Grade the rubric rows as written (sourcing, thesis, feasibility, statement, completion) rather than the artist chosen; any verified, appropriately researchable artist is an acceptable choice.

Quiz answer key ("Research & Proposal Basics")

1-B · 2-B · 3-True · 4-C · 5-C · 6 (Research summary→names the artist, works studied, and sources used; Thesis→one sentence stating what the project will do and why; Media plan→names the materials or techniques and the reasoning behind them; Sketches→test the idea as an image before committing to it) · 7-B.

assignments.title: The Abstraction Ladder
assignments.html:
This sketch is a practice rung, not a finished artwork. The goal is to make each step a clear, deliberate move from the one before it (about 20 to 30 minutes total).

Choose one simple object with a clear silhouette (an apple, a leaf, a mug, a single flower). On one sheet, take it through all four stages, left to right:

  1. Realistic. Draw it from direct observation: true outline, proportion, and any distinctive detail.
  2. Simplified. Redraw it using only its major shapes. Remove small details, but keep the true proportions and silhouette.
  3. Stylized. Redraw it again, exaggerating one quality on purpose (a curve, a color choice, a line weight), applied consistently across the whole shape.
  4. Non-representational. Take just the shapes and colors from your stylized version and rearrange or isolate them so the connection to the original object is no longer obvious on its own.

Label each stage.

Submit

Photograph your sheet in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S09_AbstractionLadder_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • All four stages are present and labeled
  • Each stage shows a clear, deliberate change from the one before it
  • Genuine effort and honest looking are visible in the realistic stage

assignments.title: Cropping & Magnification
assignments.html:
On one sheet, complete both parts (about 20 to 30 minutes).

  1. Full object. Draw your chosen object (a shell, a piece of fruit, a leaf, or similar) in full, as observed.
  2. Cropped and magnified. Choose one small, interesting part of that same object. Using a viewfinder (cut paper L-shapes, or your fingers held in an L), frame just that part and redraw it enlarged to fill your whole page.

Label which is which.

Submit

Photograph your sheet, upload as JPG or PNG, and save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S09_CroppingMagnification_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Both the full object and the cropped, magnified detail are present and labeled
  • The cropped view is enlarged to fill the page, not simply redrawn small
  • The crop chosen genuinely reads more abstractly than the full view
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: The Abstraction Path (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Sketch or photograph one small object nearby (your own choice). Open your VR space; you may choose any Location you like.

Stage 1 (about 5 min)

Using the VR drawing or note tool, record your object realistically, exactly as observed.

Stage 2 (about 7 min)

Simplify or stylize that same object, one deliberate change at a time.

Stage 3 (about 7 min)

Push it to non-representational: keep only shape and color, with no obvious link back to the object on its own.

Reflect (about 6 min)

Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "Which stage was the hardest decision to make, and why?"

Submit

Screenshot your three stages and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing each stage. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence of all three stages attempted, plus the reflection.

assignments.title: From Study to Stylization (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Choose one everyday object or natural form and create a refined observational drawing of it. Then transform that same drawing into an original stylized or abstract composition, showing the progression from your realistic study to your final piece, not only the final result.

Materials (home-accessible)

Drawing paper, pencils, colored pencils, marker, or paint; eraser. A digital drawing app is an accepted alternative.

Focus

An accurate anchor observation, a visible and deliberate abstraction process (at least two named moves: simplification, exaggeration, stylization, cropping, or magnification), and craftsmanship across every stage.

Steps

  1. Choose your subject and draw it from direct observation. This is your anchor drawing.
  2. Decide your path: the abstraction ladder, cropping and magnification, or both.
  3. Sketch two or three transitional stages that show your decisions along the way. Keep every stage.
  4. Push to your final stylized or abstract composition.
  5. Refine: critique your own progression using the four-step order (Lesson 6), then sign your work.

What makes a strong submission

  • The anchor drawing is genuinely observational and accurate
  • Every stage of the transformation is included and clearly ordered
  • At least two abstraction techniques are used on purpose and are identifiable
  • The final piece still carries the essence of the original subject
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • What object or natural form did you choose, and why?
  • Which abstraction moves did you use on purpose, and at which stage? (Name at least two.)
  • What surprised you about how far the subject could travel and still feel connected to where it started?

Submit

Photograph or export your anchor drawing, transitional stages, and final piece (as one combined image or a labeled set), upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S09_StudyToStylization_LastName.

assignments.title: Storyboard It
assignments.html:
This sketch is a practice rung, not a finished artwork. Every visual storyteller plans a sequence before drawing a finished panel. Focus on honest planning, not pretty drawing. About 20 to 30 minutes.

  1. Choose a small true or invented story with a clear beginning, middle, and end.
  2. Sketch a rough storyboard of four to six small boxes, thumbnail-quality only.
  3. Label each box with its beat: Establishing, Action, or Resolution.
  4. Make sure all three beats appear somewhere in your storyboard.

Submit

Photograph your sheet in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S10_StoryboardIt_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Four to six labeled thumbnail panels are present
  • All three beats (Establishing, Action, Resolution) appear somewhere in the sequence
  • Genuine effort and a followable story are visible

assignments.title: One Frame, One Story
assignments.html:
On one sheet, sketch a single scene that tells a story without any text (about 20 to 30 minutes).

  1. Draw one figure in a clear gesture, frozen mid-action, not a generic standing pose.
  2. Add at least two setting details (objects, light, or surroundings) that add to the story.
  3. No captions, no speech bubbles, no labels. The image alone should imply what happened just before and what is about to happen next.

Submit

Photograph your sheet, upload as JPG or PNG, and save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S10_OneFrameOneStory_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • A clear, specific gesture is drawn (not a static, generic pose)
  • At least two setting details are visible and support the story
  • No text of any kind appears in the image
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: The Sequence Gallery (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Have your storyboard and the three beats (Establishing, Action, Resolution) ready. Open your VR space and load the Studio 10 gallery snapshot from Canvas. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

Part 1, Arrange (about 10 min)

The gallery snapshot holds four unordered images. Arrange them into the story order you believe is strongest, using your VR movement tool.

Part 2, Justify (about 8 min)

Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "What in each image told you where it belonged in the sequence?" In a live session, share your order and reasoning with one classmate; note where you disagreed.

Part 3, Make (about 7 min)

Use the VR drawing tool to sketch one quick establishing-beat panel of any subject in the space.

Submit

Screenshot your final order and sketch and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing what you did. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: A Visual Story (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Create a visual story or sequential artwork, three to six panels, with no text anywhere in it. Any media (drawing, painting, collage, mixed media, or a consistent digital medium). The images alone must carry the story.

Materials (home-accessible)

Drawing or painting paper/canvas of your choice, or a digital drawing app. Keep medium consistent across all panels.

Focus

Narrative clarity (a viewer with no explanation can follow the story), sequencing and composition (deliberate beats and panel arrangement), and craftsmanship.

Steps

  1. Finalize your story: one sentence each for Establishing, Action, and Resolution.
  2. Storyboard three to six panels; confirm every beat appears somewhere.
  3. Check for text creep: replace any caption-dependent moment with a visual clue (gesture, object, setting detail).
  4. Lock your composition, palette, and medium before starting final panels; hold them consistent throughout.
  5. Draw or paint your final panels.
  6. Run the cover test on a reader who does not know your story; refine any panel that confused them.
  7. Run a critique (describe, analyze, interpret, judge) on your own sequence (Lesson 6) and make one meaningful revision.
  8. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork

  • A viewer with zero explanation can follow the whole story with no text
  • Beats and panels are deliberately arranged; composition is strong throughout
  • Style, palette, and technique stay consistent panel to panel
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • What story did you tell, and why did you choose it?
  • Which storytelling tools did you use on purpose, and where? (Name at least two: sequencing, beats, gesture, setting, implied time.)
  • What surprised you, or what would you do differently?

Submit

Photograph or export your finished panels as JPG or PNG (a single combined image or one file per panel, teacher's choice), upload, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file(s) to your portfolio: SA2_S10_VisualStory_LastName.

assignments.title: Hierarchy Thumbnails
assignments.html:
This sketch is a practice rung, not a finished poster. Designers thumbnail before they commit. Focus on honest testing of hierarchy, not a polished result. Do all three parts on one sheet (about 20 to 30 minutes total).

  1. One-dominant-element thumbnail. Pick any short message (real or invented). Sketch a tiny poster box with ONE word or shape as the clear dominant element, huge, and everything else small.
  2. Grid-based thumbnail. Same message. Sketch a simple 3x3 grid first, then place the same dominant element and supporting details inside grid cells, aligned to shared edges.
  3. Z-path check. Trace the Z-path (top-left, top-right, diagonal down, bottom-right) across Thumbnail 2 with a pencil line. Mark one adjustment you would make so the most important information sits on that path.

Label each part.

Submit

Photograph your sheet in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S11_HierarchyThumbnails_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • All three thumbnails are present and labeled
  • One dominant element is clearly identifiable in each relevant thumbnail
  • A Z-path adjustment is marked and makes sense
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Typeface Mood Specimens
assignments.html:
On one sheet, hand-letter (or cut-and-glue print type) the same short word or phrase three times, in three different letter styles chosen to match three different moods (for example: serious, urgent, playful, elegant, calm). About 20 to 30 minutes.

For each of the three versions, label: - The mood you intended - One specific design choice that creates it (for example: heavy weight, serif feet, flowing script, tight letter spacing)

Submit

Photograph your sheet, upload as JPG or PNG, and save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S11_TypeSpecimens_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Three distinct letter styles are attempted, not the same style repeated
  • Each is labeled with an intended mood and a specific design choice
  • Genuine effort and experimentation are visible

assignments.title: The Poster Wall (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Have your one-sentence message and your chosen thumbnail ready. Open your VR space and load the Studio 11 gallery snapshot from Canvas, or use any Location that lets you place images on a wall. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

Part 1, Lay out your hierarchy (about 10 min)

Place your thumbnail on a wall at a realistic poster distance. Step back as far as the space allows and note what your own eye reads first, second, and last.

Part 2, Test readability (about 8 min)

Walk to the far end of the room. Can you still read your dominant word or phrase? If not, note what you would enlarge or simplify.

Part 3, Make (about 7 min)

Use the VR drawing or note tool to sketch one quick alternative hierarchy arrangement of the same message.

Submit

Screenshot your test or sketch and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing what you found. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: Poster With a Purpose (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Design an original poster communicating a message, event, or social cause of your choosing. Digital or hand-rendered.

Materials (home/online accessible)

Any drawing/painting media, or a free digital design tool such as Canva or Pixlr E (no purchase or install required).

Focus

Hierarchy and layout (one dominant element, a grid, alignment), typography (typeface mood, contrast, legibility), and craftsmanship.

Steps

  1. Write your one-sentence message and identify your audience.
  2. Thumbnail three layout options using hierarchy and grid tools, building at least one thumbnail directly in Canva or Pixlr E (free, no install); pick the strongest.
  3. Run the two-second test on your chosen thumbnail with another person.
  4. Build your final poster in Canva, Pixlr E, or by hand: one dominant element, a grid-organized layout, one or two typefaces matched to the message's mood.
  5. Refine based on a second two-second test; critique your own work (Lesson 6).
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork

  • One clear dominant element leads the eye; the message reads in about two seconds
  • Layout is organized on a grid, with consistent alignment
  • Typeface choice matches the message's mood and stays legible at a distance
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • What message, event, or cause did you choose, and who is the audience?
  • Which design tools did you use on purpose, and where? (Name at least two.)
  • What did the two-second test reveal, and what would you do differently?

Submit

Photograph or export your finished poster as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S11_PosterWithAPurpose_LastName.

assignments.title: Expressive/Geometric Study
assignments.html:
This sketch is a practice rung, not a finished artwork. Focus on honestly trying both families of non-objective mark-making, not on a pretty result (about 10 to 15 minutes total).

  1. Choose one emotion (any emotion: excitement, boredom, dread, relief).
  2. On the left half of one page, make an expressive study: work fast, let your hand's speed and pressure change with the feeling, and do not plan the marks before you make them.
  3. On the right half of the same page, make a geometric study of the same emotion: work slow and deliberate, choose two or three basic shapes, and decide their size and position before you draw them.

Label each half with the family name and the emotion.

Submit

Photograph your page in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S12_ExpressiveGeometric_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Both halves are present and labeled with family name and emotion
  • The expressive half shows varied, fast, unplanned marks
  • The geometric half shows planned, hard-edged, measured shapes
  • Genuine effort and honest exploration are visible

assignments.title: Composing with Pure Elements
assignments.html:
Create one small non-objective study (about 15 to 20 minutes) that deliberately uses all three tools from Lesson 4:

  1. Rhythm: repeat a shape with some variation (size, spacing, or color) so the eye has a beat to follow.
  2. Balance: choose symmetrical or asymmetrical balance on purpose, so the visual weight feels intentional, not accidental.
  3. Color emotion: pick your colors for the feeling they carry, not by default.

No recognizable object anywhere in the piece. Label in the margins which tool is doing which job.

Submit

Photograph your page, upload as JPG or PNG, and save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S12_PureElements_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Rhythm, balance, and a deliberate color choice are all present and labeled
  • No recognizable object appears in the study
  • Genuine effort and intentional choices are visible

assignments.title: Paint a Feeling (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Have your chosen idea or emotion and the vocabulary from Lessons 3 and 4 ready. Open your VR space and load the Studio 12 gallery snapshot from Canvas. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

Part 1, Critique (about 8 min)

Stand in front of one non-objective work in the gallery. Critique it, running the four steps: 1. Describe: what shapes, colors, and marks are literally there? 2. Analyze: which tools (rhythm, balance, color) is the artist using, and how? 3. Interpret: what feeling or idea does the work seem to carry? 4. Judge: does it succeed, and why?

Part 2, Reflect (about 7 min)

Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "If I had to express my chosen feeling using only shape and color, with no subject, what is the first choice I would make?" In a live session, share and respond to one classmate.

Part 3, Make (about 10 min)

Use the VR drawing or building tool to create a quick non-objective sketch expressing your chosen idea using pure shape and color. No recognizable objects allowed.

Submit

Screenshot your notes or sketch and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing what you made and why. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: An Idea Without a Subject (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Choose one idea or emotion (something like tension, calm, chaos, or hope) and create an abstract/non-objective artwork expressing it through the elements of art. No recognizable object anywhere in the finished piece.

Materials

Any 2D media (paint, colored pencil, marker, collage, or digital). A digital drawing or design app is an accepted alternative to physical materials.

Focus

Deliberate use of rhythm, balance, and color to carry the chosen idea, plus a clear choice of expressive, geometric, or blended mark-making.

Steps

  1. Choose your idea or emotion and decide whether it calls for expressive marks, geometric shapes, or a deliberate mix.
  2. Thumbnail three quick non-objective compositions exploring rhythm, balance, and color for your idea; pick the strongest.
  3. Block in the major shapes lightly on your final surface.
  4. Build rhythm, check balance, and commit to color choices that carry the emotion. Work the whole surface.
  5. Refine: critique your own work using the four-step method (Lesson 6), and resist adding any recognizable object.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork

  • No recognizable subject anywhere; the idea is carried entirely by line, shape, and color
  • Rhythm, balance, and color are used deliberately, not accidentally
  • A clear, personal idea or emotion comes through
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • What idea or emotion did you choose, and why does it matter to you?
  • Which tools did you use on purpose, and where? (Name at least two: expressive or geometric marks, rhythm, balance, color emotion.)
  • What surprised you, or what would you do differently?

Submit

Photograph or export your finished artwork as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S12_IdeaWithoutSubject_LastName.

assignments.title: Four Devices
assignments.html:
This sketch is a practice rung, not a finished artwork. Surrealists generated many quick ideas before committing to one. Focus on clearly showing each device, not on polish (about 20 to 30 minutes total).

Choose one ordinary object from your Impossible List (Lesson 1). Sketch it four times, once for each device:

  1. Dislocation. Place the object in a setting where it does not belong. Keep the object itself completely ordinary.
  2. Impossible scale. Draw the object at a dramatically wrong size next to something that shows scale clearly (a person, a doorway, a chair).
  3. Metamorphosis. Show the object transforming into, or fusing with, a second form.
  4. Dream logic. Invent one consistent rule involving the object and sketch that rule once.

Label each thumbnail with its device name.

Submit

Photograph your sheet in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S13_FourDevices_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • All four thumbnails present and correctly labeled
  • Each thumbnail clearly demonstrates its named device
  • Genuine effort and idea generation are visible (not four versions of the same idea)

assignments.title: Render the Unreal
assignments.html:
Choose your strongest thumbnail from Skill Builder 1 and render it fully in value (about 25 to 35 minutes).

  1. Set one light source and commit to its direction before you shade anything.
  2. Sight the proportions of the real, observed parts of your object against each other.
  3. Build a full value range through all five light zones (highlight, midtone, core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow).
  4. Add one texture cue for the object's material (metal, cloth, stone, skin, etc.).

Label the surrealist device you used.

Submit

Photograph your sheet, upload as JPG or PNG, and save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S13_RenderUnreal_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • One consistent light source is applied across the whole sketch
  • A full value range (not just outline) is visible
  • At least one clear texture cue is present
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: The Dream Gallery (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Have your vocabulary (dislocation, impossible scale, metamorphosis, dream logic) and the four DAIJ steps ready. Open your VR space and load the Studio 13 gallery snapshot from Canvas. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

Part 1, Critique (about 10 min)

Move close to one dreamlike work that pulls your eye. Using your VR note tool, place short notes running DAIJ: 1. Describe: what is literally shown? 2. Analyze: which surrealist device is doing the most work? Is the light source consistent? 3. Interpret: what does this artist's dream let them say that a realistic scene could not? 4. Judge: does it succeed, and why?

Part 2, Reflect (about 8 min)

Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "What does this artist's dream let them say that a realistic scene could not?" In a live session, share and respond to one classmate.

Part 3, Make (about 7 min)

Use the VR building or drawing tool to place one ordinary object at an impossible scale inside the gallery space.

Submit

Screenshot your notes or scene and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing what you did. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: Dream Worlds (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Create a surreal artwork that combines realistically rendered elements in an impossible relationship. Use one clear surrealist device (dislocation, impossible scale, metamorphosis, or dream logic) and render it with the same care you would give an observational drawing.

Materials (home-accessible)

Drawing paper, graphite, charcoal, or color media of your choice. A digital drawing app with value control is an accepted alternative.

Focus

A clear, singular surrealist concept; observation and rendering (accurate proportion on real elements, a single consistent light source, a full value range); and craftsmanship.

Steps

  1. Choose your central idea and the one device it relies on most. Write it as one sentence.
  2. Decide your single light source and commit to it for the whole piece.
  3. Thumbnail two compositions; pick the strongest.
  4. Sight the proportions of every object, real or impossible, and block in the composition.
  5. Build value through all five light zones on every object, using the same light source throughout.
  6. Refine: push your darkest darks, unify the light logic, critique your own work (Lesson 6).
  7. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork

  • One surrealist device is clear, specific, and fully committed to
  • A single, consistent light source is applied across every object, real or impossible
  • Real, observed elements are drawn with accurate proportion
  • The impossible element is rendered as carefully as the rest of the piece
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • What is the impossible relationship in your image, and which device is it built on?
  • What real, observed truth or feeling were you trying to tell through this dream?
  • Where did you work hardest to make the impossible convincing?

Submit

Photograph or export your finished artwork as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S13_DreamWorlds_LastName.

assignments.title: Image/Text Thumbnails
assignments.html:
This sketch is a practice rung, not a finished artwork. Pick any low-stakes issue for practice (school lunch lines, phone use, a local park, or similar). Work through all three parts on one sheet (about 20 to 30 minutes total).

  1. Long version. Write your idea as a full sentence or two, no editing yet.
  2. Slogan cut. Cut it down through two rounds of editing until it reads in under two seconds. Write the final slogan clearly.
  3. Three thumbnails. Sketch three small, fast layout options pairing a simple image idea with your slogan. Label the audience you have in mind for each.

Submit

Photograph your sheet in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S14_ImageTextThumbnails_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Long version, cut slogan, and three labeled thumbnails are all present
  • Each thumbnail names an audience
  • Genuine effort and honest editing are visible (the slogan is shorter than the long version)

assignments.title: Fact/Opinion Audit
assignments.html:
Take the slogan you drafted in Skill Builder 1 (or write a new one for a cause you are considering for your Studio Project). Complete both parts (about 20 minutes).

  1. List every claim. Write out every factual or implied claim in your slogan and any supporting text.
  2. Label each claim. Mark each one Fact (checkable) or Opinion (a judgment). For each Fact, note where the information came from or how you would check it. For each Opinion, confirm it targets an idea, policy, or habit, not a person or group.

Submit

Upload your audit as a photo of a handwritten page or a typed document. Save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S14_FactOpinionAudit_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Every claim in the slogan/text is listed and labeled
  • Facts include a source or a way to check them
  • Opinions are confirmed as targeting an idea or policy, not a person
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Test Your Message (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Have your slogan, your fact/opinion audit, and one thumbnail ready. Enter your VR space and choose any gallery or open Location you like.

Part 1, Design check (about 8 min)

Place or display your thumbnail at a distance, the way a poster would actually be seen. Step back until it is small in your view. Can you still read the slogan? Does the image still register?

Part 2, Audience test (about 10 min)

Imagine explaining your piece to someone who disagrees with you. Speak (record a short voice note) or write two or three sentences of what you would tell them, arguing the idea, not the person.

Part 3, Revise (about 7 min)

Based on the distance test and audience test, note one change to make before you finalize your piece.

Submit

Screenshot your VR setup or your notes and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing what you did and what you changed. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: A Cause Worth Making (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Create an original artwork addressing a contemporary issue or cause that is important to you (school-appropriate). Combine image and text to make a fair, honest argument aimed at a specific audience.

Materials

Any 2D medium (drawing, painting, collage, digital design). All imagery must be your own photography, drawing, or design; see the AI-awareness note in Lesson 5 if you use any AI tool at any stage.

Focus

Message and audience (image and text depend on each other; the audience is deliberate), responsible commentary (fact vs. opinion kept straight; the idea or policy is the target, not a person), and craftsmanship.

Steps

  1. Choose your cause and write your one honest sentence.
  2. Name your audience: who specifically needs to see this?
  3. Pair with one classmate who chose a related cause. Compare your one-sentence issue statements and decide whether your two pieces will hang as a connected pair in the final exhibition, or whether you'll combine them into one shared piece. (Mirrors Lesson 5, Part 2, Step 2b, the one deliberate exception to this course's solo-work rule; see _REVISION-BRIEF.md §8.)
  4. Run the fact/opinion check on your claims.
  5. Cut your slogan through the three-pass editing process.
  6. Thumbnail three layout options; choose the strongest.
  7. Build your final piece, then critique your own work and run the fairness check (Lesson 6).
  8. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork

  • Image and text depend on each other to make the argument, not a picture with a caption
  • The audience is clear from the choices made in image, text, and tone
  • Every factual claim is one the student could defend if asked; the piece argues an idea or policy, not a person
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • What cause did you choose, and why does it matter to you?
  • Which tools did you use on purpose, and where? (Name at least two: image-text combination, slogan economy, audience, the fact/opinion check.)
  • Did you use AI at any stage? Disclose plainly, per Lessons 4 and 5.

Submit

Photograph or export your finished artwork as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S14_CauseWorthMaking_LastName.

assignments.title: Experiment Log
assignments.html:
This is a practice rung, not a finished artwork. You are learning a method for turning curiosity into evidence: change one thing at a time, keep everything else the same, and write down what actually happens, even if it fails.

Using scrap materials (not finished paper), run three trials of one media pairing you have never combined before (for example: ink over dry pencil, a wash over collage, printmaking ink combined with charcoal). For each trial, complete a log entry with: 1. Variable: the one thing you changed, in one sentence. 2. Control: everything you deliberately kept the same across all three trials. 3. Outcome: what actually happened, described honestly, whether it worked or not. 4. Keep or discard?: will this result inform your Studio Project, or was it useful information you will not reuse?

Submit

Photograph each scrap next to its written log entry (or type the log and attach photos separately). Upload as JPG, PNG, or PDF. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S15_ExperimentLog_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • All three trials are present with a clear variable, control, and outcome for each
  • At least one trial is logged honestly even if it did not produce the hoped-for result
  • Genuine effort and honest observation are visible

assignments.title: Combination Test
assignments.html:
On two labeled scraps, test how layering order changes a media combination.

  1. Scrap A: the default order. Build a controlled combination following the dry-to-wet, thin-to-thick order from Lesson 4 (for example: a dry pencil or collage base, then a thin wash, then a final dry accent once dry).
  2. Scrap B: break the order on purpose. Using the same materials, deliberately reverse the order (wet before dry, or thick before thin) and document what changes.

Label which scrap is which and note, in a sentence or two, what was different between them.

Submit

Photograph both scraps, upload as JPG or PNG, and save a copy to your portfolio folder: SA2_S15_CombinationTest_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Both scraps are present, labeled, and clearly show two different layering orders
  • A short written comparison of the two outcomes is included
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: The Materials Lab (VR Session)
assignments.html:
Before you enter

Have your variable-and-control vocabulary from Lesson 3 ready. Open your VR space; you may choose any Location you like.

Part 1, Run three quick digital experiments (about 12 min)

Using the VR drawing or building tool, try three fast tests, changing one variable each time. Examples: the same shape drawn with three different line weights, three different color combinations on the same form, or three arrangements of the same objects.

Part 2, Log outcomes (about 5 min)

For each of the three, note in writing or a short voice memo what you changed and what you noticed. Which result surprised you most?

Submit

Screenshot your three quick experiments or your notes and upload it. No screenshot tool? Write two or three sentences describing what you tried. Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading

Completion. Evidence that three distinct trials were attempted and logged.

assignments.title: Risk Log: A Series of Experimental Works (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Create a series of at least three finished experimental works, each combining two or more materials or techniques learned this year (for example: printmaking + collage, ink + charcoal, painting + drawing, or an earlier technique pushed further than its original Studio took it). Submit your series with your written experiment log and an artist statement on what you risked and learned.

Materials (home-accessible)

Any combination of media already used this year: graphite, charcoal, ink, watercolor or acrylic paint, collage papers, printmaking supplies. A digital art app is an accepted alternative if it allows layering multiple effects.

Focus

Genuine risk and innovation (at least one piece with a real, unknown-in-advance outcome), safe and intentional media combination, and honest process documentation.

Steps

  1. Review your Lesson 3 and 4 skill-builder logs; choose your strongest or most surprising trials to scale up.
  2. Plan two or three directions for finished pieces, deciding what stays consistent (a control) across your series.
  3. Build each piece, continuing to log what you try and what happens as you go.
  4. Refine: critique your own series (Lesson 6), including whether the risk paid off.
  5. Sign each piece. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong series

  • Each piece combines materials or techniques in a way that was genuinely uncertain, not already mastered
  • The combinations are handled safely and intentionally (see Lesson 4)
  • The written log traces specific trials to specific results
  • At least one piece pushes into a dimensional or fiber-based technique (for example built-up modeling paste, torn fabric, or stitched thread layered into the surface)
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the series is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • Which materials or techniques did you combine, and what genuine risk did that combination carry?
  • What actually happened? Name at least one result you did not expect.
  • What would you carry forward from this Studio, and what would you do differently next time?

Submit

Photograph or export your finished series (3+ images) as JPG or PNG, upload them along with your written experiment log, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the files to your portfolio: SA2_S15_RiskLog_LastName.

assignments.title: Research Notes
assignments.html:
Choose one artist to research for your Capstone proposal. It can be an artist, style, or subject you have been drawn to all year, or one you discover while browsing the approved sources in Lesson 3. This is a research log, not a finished essay. Focus on sourced, traceable facts.

Your notes should include: 1. Your chosen artist's name, and one or two specific verified works (title and date) you studied. 2. At least two approved sources (from the Lesson 3 list: a museum collection, a teaching site such as Smarthistory or Khan Academy, or a scholarly database such as JSTOR), each with what you learned from it. 3. At least three facts you can trace to a source: for example, a date, a technique, or a documented statement by the artist. Note where each one came from. 4. One open question you still have about the artist that you may want to answer before Lesson 4.

Submit

Type your notes directly into the text box, or upload a typed document. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S16_ResearchNotes_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • Artist named with at least one specific, dated work
  • At least two approved sources named and used
  • At least three facts are traceable to a named source, not left unsourced

These are quick, rough tests, not finished drawings. Their job is to show whether your idea works as an image before you write your proposal around it.

  1. Keep each thumbnail small (a few inches).
  2. Try two genuinely different approaches to the same idea (for example, a different arrangement, a different vantage point, or a different amount of the subject shown).
  3. Label each thumbnail with one phrase describing what it tests.

Submit

Photograph your sheet in good light. Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive portfolio folder: SA2_S16_ThumbnailSketches_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort)

  • At least two distinct thumbnail sketches are present
  • Each is labeled with what it tests
  • Genuine effort and honest exploration are visible, not a single repeated idea

Part 2, Walk and narrate (about 6 min)

Part 3, Exit

assignments.title: The Capstone Proposal (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Research an artist of your choosing (using the approved sources), and write a proposal for the original studio project you will build in Studio 17. Your submission is one Word document containing all of the following:

  1. Research summary (one short paragraph): your artist, one or two specific verified works, and the approved sources you used.
  2. Thesis (one sentence): what your proposed project will do, the device you are borrowing from your researched artist, and your own twist.
  3. Media plan (a short list): the specific materials or techniques from this year you intend to use, and why each fits your thesis.
  4. Sketches (embedded images): your two or more thumbnail sketches, photographed or scanned into the document, each with a one-sentence caption.

Materials (home-accessible)

Microsoft Word (M365), your Skill Builder 1 research notes, your Skill Builder 2 thumbnail sketches (photographed to embed).

Focus

Research and sourcing, thesis clarity, feasible media planning, and the beginning of artistic voice.

Steps

  1. Open a new Word document. Build the four parts in order: research, thesis, media plan, sketches.
  2. Photograph or scan your thumbnails and insert them with captions.
  3. Refine your thesis until it names your subject, your borrowed device, and your own twist (Lesson 4/6).
  4. Run the critique process on your own draft (Lesson 6) and revise anything still vague.
  5. Sign your document. Every finished proposal carries its artist's name, just as a finished artwork does.

What makes a strong proposal

  • The researched artist and at least three facts are traceable to approved sources
  • The thesis is specific, arguable, and names a real intention, not a vague preference
  • The media plan is feasible and clearly connects to the thesis
  • The sketches visibly test the thesis, not an unrelated idea
  • The document is complete, well organized, and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

  • Why this artist and this subject, specifically, out of everything you could have chosen?
  • What do you hope your finished Capstone will do that your researched artist's work does not?
  • What is the biggest risk or unknown in this plan right now, and how do you intend to handle it?

Submit

Upload your Word document, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S16_CapstoneProposal_LastName.

Circle the one you are choosing. 2. Milestones. A numbered list of 3 to 5 milestones for your build, each with one sentence defining what "done" means at that stage, and a deadline inside this Studio's two weeks. 3. Materials list. What you need, confirmed as home-accessible or already on hand. 4. Time budget. Your estimated hours per milestone, checked against the studio time you actually have this Studio.

  2. Analyze: which Elements or Principles are working as planned? Which are weaker?
  3. Interpret: does it still read as the idea from your proposal?
  4. Judge: name the ONE change that would most improve your next work session.

Part 2, Critique walk (about 10 min)

Part 3, Reflect (about 5 min)

assignments.title: The Capstone Artwork (Studio Project + Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Complete a large-scale, self-directed artwork from your approved Studio 16 proposal. This is your Capstone: the one artwork meant to show everything you have become as an artist across this course.

Materials

Whatever your approved proposal specifies, home-accessible or already on hand, at a scale larger and more ambitious than your usual two-week Studio project.

Focus

Faithful, ambitious execution of your own proposal; visible synthesis of skills from earlier Studios; craftsmanship sustained evenly across the whole piece; genuine intent.

Steps

  1. Confirm your milestone plan and time budget from Skill Builder 1 still fit.
  2. Build Milestone 1 (composition and structure) to completion before moving forward.
  3. Work each remaining milestone in order, running a critique checkpoint at each one.
  4. Refine: run a final checkpoint, address the one biggest weakness, and bring craftsmanship up to an even standard across the whole surface.
  5. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong Capstone

  • The finished piece faithfully and ambitiously realizes the approved Studio 16 proposal
  • Multiple skills from earlier Studios are visibly at work, at a mature level
  • Craftsmanship is sustained evenly across the entire piece, not concentrated in one section
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences)

assignments.html:
1. Full artist statement draft. Write a full draft of your artist statement covering your whole year (not one piece): where you started, what changed, why you curated your show this way, and where that leaves you now. Aim for about four short paragraphs.
  2. Two photographed works. Photograph or export two works from your curated short list to a professional standard: even light with no glare, camera straight-on (not angled), tightly cropped to just the artwork, saved at full resolution.

assignments.html:

Part 1, Hang your show (about 10 min)

Part 2, Give a docent walkthrough (about 10 min)

Part 3, Reflect (about 5 min)

Submit

Grading

assignments.title: Final Exhibition (Studio Project + Full Artist Statement)
assignments.html:
Curate a final body of work from across all 18 Studios, write a full artist statement, and present both as one professional digital exhibition: a slide deck (PowerPoint) or a web-style gallery document. This is not new artwork. It is the finishing move on everything made this year.

Tools

Build in PowerPoint (see the optima-m365 guidance) for a slide-deck exhibition, or a Word document laid out gallery-style if your teacher has approved an alternate format.

Required parts

  1. Title slide/section: your name, a title for your exhibition (not "Final Project"), and the year.
  2. 6 to 10 curated works in a deliberate sequence, one work per slide/section, image shown clearly and unobstructed.
  3. A complete wall label with every work: title, medium, Studio and date, and a one-line context note.
  4. A full artist statement at the end (about four paragraphs): where you started the year, what changed and where the evidence is, why you curated and sequenced the show this way, and where that leaves you now.

What makes a strong exhibition

  • The selection feels deliberate, not just "everything I made"
  • The sequence builds a clear sense of growth or argument
  • Every label is complete and consistent in format
  • Images are evenly lit, straight-on, cropped tight, and full resolution
  • The statement is specific (names real Studios and real changes), not generic

Submit

Upload your finished exhibition file (PowerPoint or Word). If your statement is not embedded in the file, also paste it into the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: SA2_S18_FinalExhibition_LastName.
